questions.q: Why does the network layer get deployed before any compute or storage resource?
options: Cloud providers charge more if storage is deployed first
Compute resources can be moved between networks freely, so order never matters
It's simply a convention with no technical reason behind it
Compute and storage resources have a hard dependency on a subnet to attach to at creation time
questions.explain: A VM or EC2 instance can't be created without a subnet to attach to — az vm create and aws ec2 run-instances both require network arguments.

questions.q: What is the real deployment order this lesson describes?
options: There is no required order — all resources can be created in any sequence
Compute first, then storage, then network configuration as cleanup
Storage, then compute, then network, in that order
Resource group, then VNet/VPC, then subnets, then NSGs/security groups, then compute and storage
questions.explain: Each layer depends on the one before it: a subnet needs a VNet, an NSG attaches to a subnet, and compute attaches to all of it.

questions.q: What happens if you run az vm create without specifying a VNet or subnet, and no default VNet exists in the resource group?
options: The command fails with an error requiring --subnet/--vnet-name
The command succeeds and prompts you to add a network later
Azure silently creates the VM with no network connectivity at all
The VM is created and automatically assigned to a random existing VNet
questions.explain: Azure requires a VNet/subnet to exist — the create call errors out rather than creating a VM with nowhere to attach.

questions.q: Why does deploying a VM before the real network exists end up costing more time, not less?
options: A running VM's network interface can't simply be reassigned to a different VNet, forcing a teardown and recreate
VMs deployed into a default VNet run slower than normal
There's no actual extra cost — it's exactly as fast either way
Azure charges a penalty fee for deploying resources out of order
questions.explain: Once a VM exists in one VNet, moving it to another means deleting and recreating it — deploy, discover, delete, redeploy is slower than planning the network first.

questions.q: What does a default VNet or default VPC provide?
options: An auto-created network from Azure or AWS, convenient for quick tests but the wrong choice for production
A backup network used only during disaster recovery
A security feature that blocks all traffic until configured
A network that automatically matches whatever architecture diagram you designed
questions.explain: Azure and AWS each provide a default network for convenience, but production deployments build a custom VNet/VPC on purpose instead.
